intro: Every tax stream coming in and every loan going out, for Arkadelphia and Clark County, with what each one has cost. Every figure links to the document it came from. Where a number isn't sourced yet, the page says so.

sales.label: Clark County
sales.note: Includes the 0.5% EDCCC half-cent and the 0.5% road-bond pledge

rates.property_note: Property tax inside Arkadelphia city limits is 59.75 mills, about $1,195 a year on a $100,000 home before the homestead credit. The school district takes 47.65 of those mills, the county 7.1, and the city 5.0.

edccc.summary: A countywide half-cent sales tax, 100% remitted to the Economic Development Corporation of Clark County "to be used solely for economic development." Voters approved it June 12, 2007 for seven years and renewed it March 11, 2014 and June 8, 2021 for seven more each.
edccc.gaps: 2007 (the tax's first months) has no separate figure in that year's audit, and the 2024 county audit is not yet published. Who received the money, and on what terms, is not public. That is Docket #5.

city_sales.summary: The city's own sales-tax revenue into its General Fund. Voters added a cent in 2019, and revenue nearly tripled.

debts.what: 2021 bonds refinanced the 2015 bonds that built a new middle and elementary school; 2022 bonds built a new elementary school (opened 2024)
debts.paid_by: The 17.65 debt mills voted at the 2015 school election
debts.cost: $43,307,031 in principal and interest still owed at June 30, 2024, on $32,590,000 of principal — about $10.7 million of that is interest

debts.what: A new high school and other school facilities, due July 2028
debts.paid_by: 3 new mills (44.65 to 47.65) and 2 shifted mills, voted November 18, 2025
debts.cost: Interest over the life of these bonds is not yet summed on this page

debts.what: Road improvements, including the Clark County Truck Bypass
debts.cost: $1,249,445 in interest over the life of the bonds; $7,760,000 principal still owed at the end of 2023

debts.what: Capital Improvement Refunding and Improvement Revenue Bonds, plus equipment loans (sanitation trucks, a street sweeper, a fire truck, an excavator)
debts.paid_by: City franchise fees (bonds); the General Fund and other funds (equipment)
debts.cost: $3,660,915 in total city long-term debt at the end of 2024, including $3,025,000 on the bonds

debts.what: A line of credit "to provide financing for general purposes of City government"
debts.paid_by: The General Fund; the city assigned "the revenue generated by the 2019 sales tax as a collateral"

debts.borrowed: $6,880,375 still owed at the end of 2023
debts.paid_by: Water and sewer rates, not taxes

arithmetic.lead: The half-cent has sent $25,431,732 to economic development from 2008 through 2023. Over roughly the same years, the school district borrowed for new buildings and still owes about $10.7 million in interest on its 2021 and 2022 bonds alone. Saved instead of borrowed, the half-cent's 16 audited years add up to about 73% of the $35.05 million in those two bond issues.
limits: The half-cent is legally dedicated to economic development by its ballot. The school district is a separate government and can't receive it. Using it any other way would take a new vote.
Saving first means waiting 15 to 20 years for a building that borrowing delivers now. That's a real tradeoff, and different people will weigh it differently.
This page shows what the money added up to. It doesn't judge whether the economic-development spending paid off. That can't be judged until the recipients and results are public.
arithmetic.decision: The half-cent's current seven-year term began with the June 2021 vote, so the next renewal would fall around 2028. That vote is when residents decide.
